plan.contextChunk: This figure contains six panels (a)–(f) illustrating the operation of insertion sort on an array of six integers. Each panel shows a horizontal array of six cells indexed 1 through 6 above the cells. Gray cells to the left of the current key represent the already-sorted subarray; the current key is shown in a black cell with white text; white cells to the right remain unsorted. Curved arrows below the array indicate element movements: a bold black arrow points to the slot where the key will be inserted, while lighter gray arrows indicate elements shifting one position to the right to make room. Panel (a) shows the initial array [5, 2, 4, 6, 1, 3] with key 2 at position 2 moving left past 5. Panel (b) shows key 4 at position 3 being inserted into sorted subarray [2, 5]. Panel (c) shows key 6 at position 4 requiring no movement as it is already the largest element in the sorted prefix. Panel (d) shows key 1 at position 5 shifting four elements rightward to reach position 1. Panel (e) shows key 3 at position 6 shifting three elements rightward to reach its correct position. Panel (f) shows the final sorted array [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6] with no black cell and no arrows. This figure illustrates the insertion sort algorithm step by step, demonstrating how each key is extracted and inserted into its correct position within the growing sorted subarray to its left.

interactionPlan.concept: Insertion sort grows a sorted prefix one key at a time by comparing the key leftward and shifting larger elements right until the key's correct slot is found.
elements: horizontal array of 6 labeled cells with indices 1–6 above each cell
cell values 5, 2, 4, 6, 1, 3 (initial array)
gray-filled cells marking the already-sorted prefix
black cell with white text marking the current key
white cells to the right marking the unsorted remainder
curved arrows below the array: one bold black arrow pointing to the key's insertion slot, lighter gray arrows showing elements shifting one position right
panel label indicating current pass (a)–(f)

interactions.label: Implement insertion sort

api.does: true when A[i] > A[j] — highlights both cells during replay
moves the element at index i one position left — the ONLY way to reorder elements
mark index i as the current key (renders its cell black with white text)
extend the gray sorted-prefix shading to include index i
attach a learner comment to the current replay frame

interactions.frame: the whole 6-cell array with index labels, the active key in black, the sorted prefix in gray, the compared/shifted indices highlighted, and the curved movement arrow for any shift
interactions.success_check: the final array reads 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and every frame only mutated the array via shift

demo_steps.title: Key 2 moves one slot
demo_steps.narration: The first key (2, black cell) is compared with 5; since 5 > 2 it shifts right and 2 lands in slot 1 — panels (a) to (b).

demo_steps.title: Key 6 needs no shift
demo_steps.narration: When the key (6) is larger than everything in the sorted prefix, the first comparison fails and zero shifts occur — panel (c) shows the arrow collapsing.

demo_steps.title: Key 1 sweeps the whole prefix
demo_steps.narration: Key 1 is smaller than all four sorted elements, so four consecutive shifts ripple rightward before it lands in slot 1 — the long arrow chain of panel (d).

demo_steps.title: Sorted
demo_steps.narration: After key 3 is inserted, the gray prefix covers the whole array: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 — panel (f).

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Each key only needs to travel left past the elements larger than itself — the number of shifts per key is exactly the number of inversions it participates in, which is why already-nearly-sorted input is cheap.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Six equal-width rectangular cells in a row, indices 1–6 centered above each cell, values in large serif numerals. Sorted prefix cells filled light gray; current key cell filled black with bold white numeral; untouched cells white with thin black borders. Below the array draw curved arcs: one thick black arc with arrowhead landing on the insertion slot, and thin gray arcs with arrowheads under each shifted element pointing one cell right. Panel indicator (a)–(f) at left of the row updates as replay advances. Keep the look monochrome/textbook (black, white, gray) matching CLRS Figure 2.2.

discrepancies: the guided demo only covers 4 of the 6 source panels — it steps (a) → (c) → (d) → (f), skipping panels (b) (key 4 inserted between 2 and 5) and (e) (key 3 inserted at the end), so the full pass sequence of the source is not shown

the step for panel (c) draws no arrow at all, while the source panel (c) shows a small collapsed arrow below the black key cell indicating the aborted comparison; the narration even references 'the arrow collapsing' that isn't visible

in source panel (d) the bold arrow spans the full width from slot 5 back to slot 1 with four gray shift arrows; the generated chain of gray arcs plus one bold arc is shallower and less visually emphatic than the source's sweeping multi-arrow cascade
the six-panel comparative layout of the source is replaced by a single panel at a time, so the side-by-side progression of sorted-prefix growth is lost in the default view

discrepancies: The source shows all six panels (a)–(f) simultaneously in a 2×3 grid; the generated figure shows only one panel at a time behind a stepper, so the full-sequence overview is not visible at a glance (acceptable tradeoff, but changes the composition).
In panel (c) the source draws a single short black arrow pointing straight up from slot 4 (key compared once, no shift); the generated figure draws a collapsed loop arc underneath instead.

Source arrows include both a gray shift arrow and a black key arrow per panel with distinct curved trajectories; in the generated step view the bold black key arc is quite subtle relative to the gray arcs and less visually distinct than in the source.
evaluation.notes: Default state faithfully reproduces panel (a) — correct array values, gray/black cell shading, index labels, and curved shift/key arrows — and the stepper accurately covers all six panels (a)–(f) with correct per-pass states; the editable insertion-sort workbench with frame replay is a strong pedagogical addition, with only minor deviations in panel (c)'s arrow style and the loss of the simultaneous six-panel overview.
action_items: For the no-shift case (panel c), draw a short vertical black arrow pointing up at the key's slot to match the source, instead of the collapsed loop arc.
Make the bold black key-travel arc thicker or more contrasted so it reads as clearly as the source's black arrow against the gray shift arrows.
Consider an optional 'show all panels' toggle so students can see the complete (a)–(f) sequence laid out like the textbook figure.
